Look at the visible label HIDDEN SECRET here.

Urban heat islands form where pavement, roofs and walls absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, which keeps neighborhoods warmer than the countryside around them. Planners have tried reflective roofs, permeable paving, misting stations and shade structures, and each works under some conditions and fails under others. The largest synthetic comparison so far, a comparison of twelve interventions across forty cities, measured air and surface temperatures every hour for three summers and matched blocks by density, traffic and building height. Street trees cut afternoon air temperatures the most, especially on narrow streets, while reflective roofs mattered mainly for the top floors of low buildings. Misting stations cooled small plazas for a few minutes at a time but used a great deal of water, and shade sails helped at bus stops without changing the temperature of the street as a whole.
